MMOs in general suffer from a lack of keyboard and mouse as primary input devices. This is not to say they aren't available, but it is very much to say that people who want to sit on their couch with a controller either can't do what they want, or piss off the people they're playing with when they're unable to communicate.

FFXI was a group-centric game. It also had the unfortunate place in history of coming just after EQ and just before WoW, which is to say it arrived before MMO developers learned that players really do resent being harshly punished for someone else' failure. I mean, FFXI was my first MMORPG and in all of the things I did in MMORPGs after, I never resented anything anyone did in any other game more than I did in FFXI when you were counting on some asshole to execute the simplest of tasks and after he fails to do so and you find your character face down on the ground, reduced in level from the experience penalty you get for dying and unable to equip half your gear as a result, and a full 90 seconds later he types "shit sorry lol was watching tv"...well, let's just say that my experience in that game was all the anecdotal evidence I'll ever need that forcing people to group if you want to progress and then punishing them as a group for the actions of one is a fucking terrible way to design a game.

Putting an MMO on a console and a PC worked for a short while, but PC players eventually began to resent the restrictions they were required to endure because PC hardware evolved but PS2 hardware did not. By the time most people started to leave, the game looked dated and repetitive on PC.

Overall FFXI was a reflection of the times. It was, as mentioned, highly group-centric, grindy as hell, extremely unforgiving, and with a very present random influence that often meant that you could do everything right and still fail (and thus, be punished). FFXI represents a step in the direction of evolved gaming that showed developers that they are neither gods nor social engineers, and should not attempt to be either. Everything that I enjoyed in FFXI, I enjoyed because I didn't know any better. Online gaming was still in its infancy. We can all be grateful that they don't make games like that anymore.

I actually spent a lot of time playing FFXI on PC while I was waiting for WoW to come out, then we all migrated.

I had a good group of people to play with, and we did pretty well. I played a Galkan Monk if I remember the names of the races correctly, and generally had fun. But eventually I hit a point where I just couldn't care anymore. It began taking longer and longer to find groups to play with. The groups demanded you have better and better equipment, that was increasingly difficult to actually find. I remember as a monk groups demanded a specific set of bracers be equiped or they wouldn't take you. And it could only be farmed off a single mob that was insanely overfarmed. Not like it dropped reliably either. You could try getting it from the auction house, but it was always too rich for my blood.

Which brings me to my next point. I loathed the farming. And that really was the problem with MMOs pre-WoW. There was no instancing. So everyone was constantly competing for spots. And the perfect spot was so hard to find. Preferably it was a spot where nothing would spawn around it and aggro, but frequently you just made due and tried to time out how long you had before the spawn you were sitting on top of popped. I recall long stretches of the game where it was slow, tedious and frustrating to actually fight anything because the zone was jam packed and the moment a single monster spawned, 6 different groups tried to pull it at the same time.

All in all it was a far more time consuming game than I'd ever have time for now. It would take you an hour easily to find a group, travel to where you wanted to farm, and then finally begin pulling mobs. As I advanced further and further in the game, a lot of the time you'd pull one or two mobs, suffer a party wipe or near party wipe, and then someone would give up and quit, necessitating another extended wait as you spammed the chat for someone to fulfill that role.

I forget which class it was, probably white mage, but it was always in demand. And they fucking knew it. You always needed one to complete your group, and they'd practically interview YOU for the honor of taking them. They were also the first to quit the party if things ever went south because they figured they could find a better one. Ugh, it was miserable when I think back on it.

Anyways, that's how FFXI went for me.

I recall two major problems when irked playing on the PS2: Slow connection and skill training. When I played, it was in a small town in SE AR. We had "high speed" internet at a whopping 1.5 Mbps. At least, that's what I was paying for. At best, we were looking at 500 kbps. Upload time was, of course, worse, and frequently topped out at 200 kbps. So, latency was a MAJOR problem. Add to that, the fact that seemingly every action you performed other than typing into the virtual keyboard had to be sent off to the nearest server. (I think ours was in New York.) You end up with an almost unplayable game.

The problem with learning skills was that I wanted to learn blacksmithing. After investing he hours it took to get to level 10 and be told that I should consider a skill, I found that my chosen profession would require me to go to another city. I was unable to find any sort of fast travel system, so that meant that I would have to walk all the way across the continent. That put me face to face with mobs so far above my level, that it was a joke to even consider. I was able to find a high level player bord enough to 'escort' me to the city I needed to reach. (If you thought escort missions were bad before, try being the one escorted.) Any death I experienced along he way cost me, well, experience. So, it was important to keep close to my guide and not get lost. If I didn't have any questions, it was easy. If I did, typing for five minutes at a time made them seem less important.

Aside from all that, the PS2 didn't include a HDD, so the game was more expensive since a 40GB HDD had to be included to install the game on. Tack on $20/mon or whatever to play, and I had no problem dropping that game.
